brief: Career advice: 10 years in B2B sales; the #1 skill is listening; a deal was once saved by shutting up for 90 seconds on a call.
facts: deal saved by staying silent for 90 seconds on a call
original_draft:
10 years in B2B sales taught me many things.

But the #1 skill? It's not pitching. It's not negotiating. It's not objection handling.

It's listening.

Let me tell you a story. A few years ago, I was on a call with a deal that was falling apart. The prospect had concerns, and every instinct told me to jump in with answers.

Instead, I did something that felt terrifying: I shut up. For 90 full seconds.

The silence was excruciating. But in that silence, the prospect talked themselves through their own objection — and revealed the real blocker, one I never would have guessed.

We closed the deal two weeks later.

Here's what a decade in sales has taught me:
🎧 Prospects will tell you exactly how to sell to them — if you let them
🎧 Silence isn't awkward. It's powerful.
🎧 The best discovery question is sometimes no question at all

Talk less. Sell more.

What's the best sales lesson you've learned the hard way? 👇

brief: Failure story: founder shut down startup "Cartful" after 3 years; raised $1.1M; grew to 4k users but never found repeatable revenue; 3 lessons.
original_draft:
After 3 years, I've made the hardest decision of my professional life: I'm shutting down Cartful.

We raised $1.1M. We grew to 4,000 users. We poured everything we had into this company. And yet, we never found repeatable revenue.

Writing this post is painful — but I owe it to everyone who believed in us to share what I learned.

Lesson 1: Users are not customers. We celebrated signups while avoiding the harder question: who will actually pay, and why?

Lesson 2: Repeatable revenue beats everything. One-off deals feel like traction. They're not. If you can't describe your sales motion in one sentence, you don't have one.

Lesson 3: Runway is for learning, not surviving. We stretched our runway to stay alive instead of spending it to find the truth faster.

To our investors, our team, and our users: thank you. I'm sorry we couldn't get there.

Failure isn't the opposite of success. It's tuition.

On to the next chapter. 🙏

brief: Engineering manager stopped daily standups for a team of 14; replaced with async written updates; meetings down 6 hrs/week; shipping speed unchanged.
original_draft:
I stopped daily standups for my team of 14.

Yes, really. And the results surprised even me.

A few months ago, we replaced our daily standup with async written updates. Every morning, each person posts three things: what they did, what they're doing, and what's blocking them.

The results?
⏰ 6 hours of meetings eliminated per week
🚢 Shipping speed: completely unchanged
😌 Engineers report fewer interruptions and more deep work

Here's the thing nobody wants to admit: most standups aren't for the team. They're for the manager. They're a status ritual dressed up as collaboration.

Written updates turned out to be better in almost every way:
✍️ People think before they write
📚 Updates are searchable and permanent
🌍 Time zones stop mattering

Am I saying standups are always wrong? No. But if your standup feels like a status meeting, it probably is one — and your team already knows it.

Would your team survive without daily standups? Be honest. 👇

brief: Announcement: passed AWS Solutions Architect Professional exam; studied 11 weeks while working full-time; 5 practice exams.
original_draft:
I passed the AWS Solutions Architect Professional exam! ☁️🎉

11 weeks of studying. A full-time job. 5 practice exams. Countless late nights and early mornings.

This was, without a doubt, one of the hardest certifications I've ever pursued — and one of the most rewarding.

For anyone preparing for this exam, here's what worked for me:

📚 Consistency over intensity — one hour every day beats eight hours on Saturday
📝 Practice exams are everything — I took 5, and each one exposed gaps I didn't know I had
🛠️ Build, don't just read — hands-on labs made concepts stick in a way videos never could
⏰ Protect your study time like a meeting — because it is one

To everyone balancing certifications with a full-time job: it's hard, but it's absolutely possible. Your future self will thank you.

Next stop: putting this knowledge to work.

brief: Reflection on first year as an engineering manager; hardest change: measuring output by the team's work, not personal commits; 7 direct reports.
facts: first year as an engineering manager
measuring output by the team's work, not personal commits
original_draft:
One year ago, I became an engineering manager.

It's been the most humbling year of my career.

The hardest change wasn't the meetings, the 1:1s, or even the difficult conversations. It was this: learning to measure my output by my team's work — not my personal commits.

For years, my sense of accomplishment came from shipping code. Green squares. Merged PRs. Tangible progress I could point to at the end of every day.

Then suddenly, my "output" became invisible. A good week meant my 7 direct reports were unblocked, growing, and shipping — while my own contributions showed up nowhere.

It took me months to stop feeling like an impostor.

What I've learned in year one:
🌱 Your team's success is your success — full stop
🗣️ Most problems are communication problems in disguise
🧭 Clarity is the greatest gift a manager can give
⏸️ Resist the urge to jump in and fix it yourself

To every new EM struggling with the identity shift: you're not alone.

What was your hardest lesson as a first-time manager? 👇

brief: The ROI of documentation: after writing runbooks, on-call pages dropped 30% in one quarter; team of 9 SREs.
original_draft:
Want to reduce on-call pain? Write things down.

I know — documentation isn't glamorous. Nobody gets promoted for writing runbooks. But here's what happened when our team of 9 SREs finally committed to it:

On-call pages dropped 30% in a single quarter.

Not because our systems magically got better. Because our knowledge stopped living exclusively in people's heads.

Here's what we did:
📖 Every incident got a runbook entry — no exceptions
🔁 Every repeated page triggered a documentation review
🧹 We deleted outdated docs as aggressively as we wrote new ones
✅ Runbook quality became part of our definition of done

The ROI of documentation is invisible until you measure it. Fewer 2 AM wake-ups. Faster onboarding. Less bus factor. Calmer on-call rotations.

Documentation isn't a chore. It's an investment with compounding returns.

If your team is drowning in pages, don't buy another tool. Write a runbook.

brief: Remote vs hybrid: their company went hybrid (2 days in office) after 3 years fully remote; retention improved but 2 senior people quit over it.
original_draft:
After 3 years fully remote, our company went hybrid — 2 days in the office.

Here's the honest truth about how it's gone.

The good:
✅ Retention improved — our numbers are better than they've been in two years
✅ Onboarding got noticeably faster
✅ Cross-team collaboration feels easier

The hard:
❌ 2 senior people quit over the change — genuinely painful losses
❌ Trust took a hit during the transition
❌ Some days the office is half empty, and people wonder why they commuted

Here's what I've learned: there is no perfect answer to the remote vs hybrid debate. Every model has tradeoffs. Every policy will disappoint someone.

What matters is honesty. We told our team exactly why we made the change, and we accepted that some people would make a different choice for their lives. I respect that deeply.

Anyone who claims remote vs hybrid is a solved problem is selling something.

What's your company's model — and is it actually working? 👇

brief: Debate post: AI won't replace junior devs, but it changes what "junior" means; cites their team hiring 2 juniors who ship with AI pair-tools.
original_draft:
AI won't replace junior developers.

But it will completely change what "junior" means.

We recently hired 2 junior engineers on my team. Both use AI pair-programming tools daily. And here's what I've noticed: they ship production code faster than juniors did five years ago — by a wide margin.

But the skills that make them valuable have shifted:

🧠 Less: memorizing syntax, writing boilerplate
🧠 More: reviewing code critically, asking the right questions, understanding systems

The junior developer of today isn't someone who writes simple code slowly. It's someone who orchestrates AI tools, verifies their output, and learns architecture from day one.

This has huge implications:
1. Hiring rubrics built around syntax trivia are obsolete
2. Mentorship matters more, not less — judgment can't be autocompleted
3. The ladder from junior to senior is compressing

Companies that stop hiring juniors "because AI" are making a strategic mistake. They're not eliminating a cost — they're eliminating their future senior pipeline.

Are you still hiring junior devs? Why or why not? 👇

brief: Customer story: a churned customer came back after they moved from seat-based to usage-based pricing; expansion revenue up 22% since.
facts: moved from seat-based to usage-based pricing
original_draft:
Last week, something happened that made my entire month: a churned customer came back.

When they left, they told us the truth — our seat-based pricing punished them for growing their team. They were paying for licenses nobody used.

We listened. We made the leap from seat-based to usage-based pricing. It was scary. We modeled the downside a dozen times. Some advisors told us not to do it.

The results since the switch:
📈 Expansion revenue up 22%
🤝 Sales conversations now start with value, not license counts
🔄 And now — churned customers are coming back on their own

The lesson? Pricing isn't just a revenue lever. It's a statement about whose side you're on. Seat-based pricing rewarded us when customers overbought. Usage-based pricing rewards us only when our customers succeed.

Aligning your incentives with your customers' isn't just good ethics — it's good business.

Has your company changed its pricing model? What happened? I'd love to hear your story. 👇

brief: Mentoring story: mentored a bootcamp grad for 6 months; grad just got hired as a frontend dev at an insurance company; 4 mock interviews.
facts: mentored a bootcamp grad for 6 months
hired as a frontend dev at an insurance company
original_draft:
Six months ago, a bootcamp grad asked me to mentor them.

This week, they signed an offer as a frontend developer at an insurance company. 🎉

I'm not sharing this for credit — the hard work was entirely theirs. I'm sharing it because the journey taught me as much as it taught them.

What we did over 6 months:
📅 Weekly check-ins, even when progress felt slow
💻 Code reviews on real projects, not toy exercises
🎤 4 mock interviews — each one harder than the last
🧠 Honest conversations about rejection and resilience

Here's what I learned: mentorship isn't about having all the answers. It's about being consistent when someone's confidence is wavering.

The tech industry loves to debate whether bootcamp grads can make it. From where I'm standing, the answer is simple: with grit and the right support, absolutely.

If you're an experienced developer, mentor someone. One hour a week can change a career.

And to my mentee: congratulations. You earned every bit of this. 🙌
